meta.notes: Command Reference for CyberWithMadhav. Defensive use only: inventory, logging, triage and hardening on systems you own or administer. Examples were checked against the linked official docs. Linux auth log paths differ by distro (auth.log on Debian and Ubuntu, secure on RHEL family). Cisco links point to the official Cisco IOS or IOS XE command reference chapter that contains the command; scroll or search the page for the command name.

commands.what: Shows open sockets: listening ports, established connections and the process that owns each one. Modern replacement for netstat.
commands.output: One line per socket with Netid (tcp or udp), State such as LISTEN, Local Address:Port, Peer Address:Port and users:(("sshd",pid=812,fd=3)).
commands.blue: Spot unexpected listeners (for example a shell on port 4444) and map every open port to a process during triage.
commands.safety: Read only. sudo is needed to see process names for sockets owned by other users.

commands.what: Legacy tool from net-tools that lists connections, listening ports, routing tables and interface statistics.
commands.output: Columns Proto, Local Address, Foreign Address, State and PID/Program name for each listening TCP or UDP port.
commands.blue: Same use as ss on older servers and appliances where ss is not installed; compare output against your approved port list.
commands.safety: Read only. May not be installed by default on newer distributions (install net-tools or use ss).

commands.what: Shows the IP addresses, state and MAC address of every network interface.
commands.output: Brief table: interface name, UP or DOWN, and its IPv4 and IPv6 addresses with prefix length, e.g. eth0 UP 192.168.1.20/24.
commands.blue: Confirm which interfaces and addresses a host really has, and catch rogue interfaces or unexpected tunnels (tun0, wg0).
commands.safety: Read only when used with show. The add and del subcommands change configuration and need root, so avoid them on production hosts unless planned.

commands.what: Displays the kernel routing table, including the default gateway.
commands.output: Lines like default via 192.168.1.1 dev eth0 and 192.168.1.0/24 dev eth0 proto kernel scope link src 192.168.1.20.
commands.blue: Check that traffic leaves through the expected gateway and that no one has added a route that diverts traffic.
commands.safety: Read only with show. ip route add or del changes routing and can cut off remote access.

commands.what: Captures and prints network packets on an interface, with powerful filters. Can also save captures to a pcap file for Wireshark.
commands.output: One line per packet: timestamp, source IP.port > destination IP.port, protocol details such as DNS query A? example.com.
commands.blue: Verify suspicious DNS or beaconing traffic, confirm a firewall rule works and collect evidence with -w capture.pcap.
commands.safety: Capture only on networks you own or administer. Packets can contain passwords and personal data, so store pcap files securely and follow your privacy policy.

commands.what: Queries the systemd journal, the central log store on most modern Linux systems.
commands.output: Timestamped log lines for the chosen unit, e.g. sshd[1234]: Failed password for invalid user admin from 203.0.113.5 port 52144 ssh2.
commands.blue: Review SSH logins, service crashes and boot events; use -f to follow live and -p err to show only errors.
commands.safety: Read only. Reading all logs may need sudo or membership of the systemd-journal group. The service is called sshd on RHEL family systems.

commands.what: Controls and inspects systemd services, timers and other units.
commands.output: Table of UNIT, LOAD, ACTIVE, SUB and DESCRIPTION for every running service.
commands.blue: Build a baseline of running services and spot unknown ones; systemctl list-timers also reveals scheduled jobs used for persistence.
commands.safety: list and status are read only. start, stop, disable and mask change the system, so use them only on hosts you manage.

commands.what: Lists running processes with their PID, parent, owner and full command line.
commands.output: Columns UID, PID, PPID, C, STIME, TTY, TIME and CMD, with child processes drawn as a tree under their parents.
commands.blue: Find odd parent and child chains, such as a web server process that spawned a shell, and note PIDs for further checks.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Lists open files, and because sockets are files, shows which process holds which network connection.
commands.output: Columns COMMAND, PID, USER, FD, TYPE, NODE and NAME, e.g. sshd 812 root 3u IPv4 TCP *:22 (LISTEN).
commands.blue: Tie a suspicious connection to its program, or find which process still holds a deleted file open.
commands.safety: Read only. Can be slow on busy servers; sudo is needed to see processes owned by other users.

commands.what: Searches the filesystem by name, type, owner, size, permissions or modification time.
commands.output: One line per match with inode, permissions, owner, size, date and path for files changed in the last 2 days.
commands.blue: Locate recently modified configs or binaries after an incident, or files owned by a removed user account.
commands.safety: Read only, but searching the whole disk is heavy on I/O; limit the paths on production servers.

commands.what: Changes file permission bits (read, write, execute) for owner, group and others.
commands.output: No output on success. Check the result with ls -l, which should show -rw------- for the key.
commands.blue: Harden permissions on private keys, scripts and config files that contain secrets.
commands.safety: Changes the system. Avoid recursive chmod -R on system folders; a wrong mode can lock users out or expose secrets.

commands.what: Changes the owner and group of files and directories.
commands.output: No output on success. Confirm with ls -l /etc/cron.d/backup.
commands.blue: Make sure scheduled job files and service configs are owned by root so normal users cannot edit them.
commands.safety: Changes the system and needs root. Wrong ownership can break services, so record the old owner first.

commands.what: Lists all files including hidden dot files, with permissions, owner, size and date.
commands.output: Lines like drwxrwxrwt 12 root root 4096 Nov 1 10:00 . followed by each entry with its mode, owner and group.
commands.blue: Spot hidden files or scripts in /tmp, /dev/shm and home folders, and check permissions at a glance.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Shows detailed metadata for a file: size, permissions, owner, inode and access, modify and change times.
commands.output: Fields File, Size, Access: (0644/-rw-r--r--) Uid Gid, then Access, Modify, Change and Birth timestamps.
commands.blue: Build an incident timeline by checking when a sensitive file was last modified or had its metadata changed.
commands.safety: Read only, but note that some tools and the act of reading can update the access time on some filesystems.

commands.what: Computes or verifies SHA256 hashes of files.
commands.output: A 64 character hex hash followed by the file name. With -c SHA256SUMS it prints OK or FAILED per file.
commands.blue: Verify downloads against the vendor hash and look up suspicious file hashes in threat intel such as VirusTotal.
commands.safety: Read only. Uploading a hash is fine, but do not upload confidential files themselves to public scanners.

commands.what: Searches text or files for lines that match a pattern or regular expression.
commands.output: Each matching log line, e.g. Nov 1 10:02:11 web sshd[991]: Failed password for root from 198.51.100.7.
commands.blue: Hunt for failed logins, IP addresses or indicators of compromise across log files; add -c to count hits.
commands.safety: Read only. auth.log is on Debian and Ubuntu; RHEL family systems use /var/log/secure.

commands.what: Shows the history of user logins, logouts and reboots from the wtmp file.
commands.output: Lines with user, terminal, source IP or host, full login and logout times and session length; reboot entries appear too.
commands.blue: Check who logged in, from where and when; compare against working hours and known admin IPs. lastb (root) shows failed attempts.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Shows who is logged in right now, with terminal and login time.
commands.output: Lines with user, terminal such as pts/0, login time and source address, plus boot time and run level.
commands.blue: Quickly see if an unknown account or unexpected remote session is active during an incident.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Prints the user ID, group ID and all groups of a user.
commands.output: uid=1001(alice) gid=1001(alice) groups=1001(alice),27(sudo).
commands.blue: Confirm which accounts are in privileged groups like sudo, wheel or docker during an access review.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Lists the commands a user is allowed to run with sudo, as defined in sudoers.
commands.output: A Matching Defaults section, then lines like (ALL : ALL) ALL or (root) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/systemctl restart nginx.
commands.blue: Audit sudo rights during access reviews and remove broad or NOPASSWD entries that are not needed.
commands.safety: Read only. Checking another user with -U requires root. Fix findings with visudo, never by editing sudoers directly.

commands.what: Lists the scheduled cron jobs of the current user, or of another user when run as root.
commands.output: Cron lines with five time fields and a command, e.g. 0 2 * * * /usr/local/bin/backup.sh, or no crontab for alice.
commands.blue: Look for unknown scheduled commands, a common persistence spot. Also check /etc/crontab and /etc/cron.d.
commands.safety: Read only with -l. Never run crontab -r by mistake; it deletes the whole crontab without asking.

commands.what: Lists the rules in the netfilter firewall tables with packet and byte counters.
commands.output: Chains INPUT, FORWARD and OUTPUT with their policy, then numbered rules showing pkts, bytes, target, prot, source and destination.
commands.blue: Confirm the host firewall really blocks what policy says it should; counters show which rules are being hit.
commands.safety: Read only with -L. Commands like -F or -P DROP change the firewall and can lock you out of a remote server. Many systems now use nftables (nft list ruleset) or ufw.

commands.what: Shows the path packets take to a destination, hop by hop, with round trip times.
commands.output: Numbered hops with router IPs and three timing values each; * * * means a hop did not reply.
commands.blue: Find where traffic is dropped or rerouted and confirm traffic exits through the expected ISP or VPN.
commands.safety: Low risk and safe to run against public hosts. Some networks block the probes, so stars do not always mean a fault.

commands.what: PowerShell cmdlet that reads Windows event logs and ETW logs with fast filtering.
commands.output: Rows with TimeCreated, Id, LevelDisplayName and Message such as An account failed to log on.
commands.blue: Hunt failed logons (4625), successful logons (4624), new services (7045) and log clearing (1102) during triage.
commands.safety: Read only. Reading the Security log requires an elevated PowerShell session.

commands.what: Lists TCP connections and listening ports with the owning process ID.
commands.output: Table of LocalAddress, LocalPort and OwningProcess; pass the PID to Get-Process to get the program name.
commands.blue: Map every listening port to a process and spot remote connections to unfamiliar IPs.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Lists running processes with CPU, memory, ID and optional file path.
commands.output: Top 10 processes by CPU time with Name, Id, CPU seconds and full Path.
commands.blue: Find processes running from odd folders like AppData or Temp, or with names that imitate system binaries.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Lists Windows services and their status.
commands.output: Table with Status, Name and DisplayName for each running service.
commands.blue: Baseline running services and look for unfamiliar ones; attackers often install services for persistence.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Lists local user accounts on the machine.
commands.output: Table of Name, Enabled (True or False) and LastLogon date for each local account.
commands.blue: Find unexpected local accounts, accounts that should be disabled and stale accounts that never log on.
commands.safety: Read only. Available in Windows PowerShell 5.1; in PowerShell 7 it may need the Microsoft.PowerShell.LocalAccounts module.

commands.what: Lists the members of a local group.
commands.output: Table of ObjectClass (User or Group), Name such as PC01\alice and PrincipalSource.
commands.blue: Review who has local admin rights; new members of Administrators are a classic red flag.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Computes the hash of a file, SHA256 by default.
commands.output: Algorithm, Hash (64 hex characters) and Path.
commands.blue: Verify installers against vendor hashes and check suspicious files against threat intel.
commands.safety: Read only. Share hashes freely, but do not upload confidential files to public scanners.

commands.what: Lists scheduled tasks with their path and state.
commands.output: Table of TaskPath, TaskName and State (Ready or Running) for enabled tasks.
commands.blue: Look for tasks with random names or odd paths that run scripts at logon, a common persistence method.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Shows the status of Microsoft Defender Antivirus on the machine.
commands.output: True or False flags for the service and real time protection, plus the date of the last signature update.
commands.blue: Confirm protection is on and signatures are current; disabled real time protection is a strong warning sign.
commands.safety: Read only. If Defender is replaced by another antivirus product, some fields show passive or disabled.

commands.what: Command line tool to query, export and manage Windows event logs.
commands.output: The 5 newest Security events in readable text with Log Name, Source, Date, Event ID and Description.
commands.blue: Pull events on systems without PowerShell access, or export logs with wevtutil epl Security C:\IR\sec.evtx for analysis.
commands.safety: Run elevated to read the Security log. Never use wevtutil cl (clear log) on a system under investigation; it destroys evidence.

commands.what: Shows all connections and listening ports with numeric addresses and the owning process ID.
commands.output: Columns Proto, Local Address, Foreign Address, State and PID, e.g. TCP 0.0.0.0:3389 0.0.0.0:0 LISTENING 1044.
commands.blue: Match PIDs with tasklist to identify which program is talking to a suspicious remote IP.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Shows full IP configuration for every adapter: IP, MAC, gateway, DNS servers and DHCP details.
commands.output: Per adapter blocks with Physical Address, IPv4 Address, Default Gateway, DHCP Server and DNS Servers.
commands.blue: Check for tampered DNS server settings and confirm the host identity (MAC and IP) when correlating logs.
commands.safety: Read only. Avoid /release and /renew on remote machines, as they can drop your session.

commands.what: Shows the security privileges held by the current user token.
commands.output: Table of Privilege Name, Description and State (Enabled or Disabled), e.g. SeShutdownPrivilege.
commands.blue: Check that service and user accounts hold only the privileges they need; powerful ones like SeDebugPrivilege should be rare.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Lists running processes in cmd, with optional service and module details.
commands.output: Columns Image Name, PID and Services, showing which services run inside each svchost.exe.
commands.blue: Pair with netstat -ano to name the process behind a connection, and spot unknown executables.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Lists scheduled tasks from cmd, with full details in verbose mode.
commands.output: Blocks per task with TaskName, Next Run Time, Status, Task To Run, Run As User and schedule.
commands.blue: Review the Task To Run field for scripts in user folders or encoded PowerShell, both common persistence signs.
commands.safety: Read only with /query. /create, /change and /delete modify the system.

commands.what: Lists local user accounts, or shows details for one account.
commands.output: Fields such as Account active, Password last set, Last logon and Local Group Memberships.
commands.blue: Quick account review on any Windows build; check that former staff accounts are inactive.
commands.safety: Read only when viewing. Adding a password or /add changes accounts, so do that only through approved change processes.

commands.what: Displays or changes NTFS access control lists on files and folders.
commands.output: Each identity with its rights, e.g. BUILTIN\Users:(OI)(CI)(RX) and NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM:(OI)(CI)(F).
commands.blue: Audit who can read or write sensitive shares and catch Everyone or Users groups with write or full control.
commands.safety: Read only when listing. /grant, /deny and /reset change permissions; save the current ACL first with /save.

commands.what: Tests connectivity to a host, including whether a specific TCP port is reachable.
commands.output: ComputerName, RemoteAddress, RemotePort, InterfaceAlias and TcpTestSucceeded : True or False.
commands.blue: Confirm firewall rules and segmentation: a port that should be blocked must return False.
commands.safety: Low risk. Test only hosts you manage; probing many ports on other people's systems is scanning.

commands.what: PowerShell DNS lookup tool that queries any record type.
commands.output: Table of Name, Type, TTL, Section and NameExchange with Preference for each mail server.
commands.blue: Check suspicious domains from phishing mail and confirm your own SPF, DMARC (TXT) and MX records.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Windows traceroute: shows each router hop to a destination with timings.
commands.output: Numbered hops with three round trip times and the router IP; -d skips name lookups so it runs faster.
commands.blue: Find where connectivity breaks and confirm traffic goes through the expected gateway or VPN.
commands.safety: Low risk. Some routers do not answer, so a timeout hop is not always a fault.

commands.what: Shows which Windows audit policy categories are logged (success, failure or none).
commands.output: A list of categories such as Logon/Logoff with subcategories like Logon set to Success and Failure.
commands.blue: Check that logon, account management and process creation auditing are on, otherwise the events you hunt will not exist.
commands.safety: Read only with /get, but it needs an elevated prompt. /set changes audit policy, so use Group Policy for that.

commands.what: Open source network scanner that discovers hosts, open ports and service versions.
commands.output: Nmap scan report for each live host with its IP, MAC and vendor, then a summary such as 12 hosts up.
commands.blue: Build an inventory of your own network, find unknown devices and verify that only approved ports are open (nmap -sV -p 22,80,443 192.168.1.10).
commands.safety: Scan only networks and hosts you own or have written permission to test. Unauthorised scanning can attract civil liability under IT Act s.43 and criminal charges under s.66 in India.

commands.what: DNS lookup tool from ISC BIND that shows full query and answer details.
commands.output: With +short, just the answers, e.g. 10 mail.example.com. Without it, full HEADER, QUESTION and ANSWER sections with TTLs.
commands.blue: Investigate phishing domains, check SPF and DMARC records (dig TXT _dmarc.example.com) and spot DNS tampering by querying a known resolver with @.
commands.safety: Low risk. Avoid zone transfer (AXFR) attempts against servers you do not run.

commands.what: Simple DNS lookup tool available on Windows, Linux and macOS.
commands.output: The DNS server used, then a Non authoritative answer section listing mail exchanger records.
commands.blue: Quick check of a suspicious domain or of which DNS server a machine is really using.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Sends ICMP echo requests to test whether a host is reachable and measure latency.
commands.output: Reply lines with bytes, TTL and time in ms, then packet loss percentage and min, avg and max round trip.
commands.blue: Basic reachability check during incidents; TTL values can hint at the remote OS family.
commands.safety: Low risk. Do not flood hosts (ping -f) or sweep networks you do not own.

commands.what: Fetches only the HTTP response headers of a URL.
commands.output: Status line such as HTTP/2 200, then headers like content-type, server and strict-transport-security.
commands.blue: Check security headers (HSTS, CSP), redirects and server banners on your own sites, and inspect suspicious links without loading the page body.
commands.safety: Low risk, but requests reveal your IP to the server. Inspect phishing URLs from a sandbox or lab machine.

commands.what: Shows the ARP cache: IP to MAC address mappings the host has learned on the local network.
commands.output: Entries with IP address, physical (MAC) address and type (dynamic or static), grouped by interface.
commands.blue: Spot ARP spoofing, where two IPs suddenly share one MAC (often the gateway), and identify devices on your own LAN.
commands.safety: Read only. On Linux the modern equivalent is ip neigh.

commands.what: Displays the configuration currently active in RAM on the router or switch.
commands.output: Only the line vty block, e.g. line vty 0 4, transport input ssh, login local.
commands.blue: Audit device hardening: SSH only on VTY lines, no telnet, encrypted passwords, logging and NTP configured.
commands.safety: Read only but needs privileged EXEC. Output contains password hashes and SNMP strings, so never paste it publicly.

commands.what: One line summary of every interface: IP address, status and protocol state.
commands.output: Columns Interface, IP-Address, OK?, Method, Status and Protocol, e.g. GigabitEthernet0/0 192.168.1.1 YES manual up up.
commands.blue: Spot interfaces that are up but should be shut down, and confirm unused ports are administratively down.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Detailed status and counters for interfaces: errors, drops, speed, duplex and traffic rates.
commands.output: GigabitEthernet0/1 is up, line protocol is up, then MTU, bandwidth, input and output rates, CRC and error counters.
commands.blue: Sudden traffic spikes or rising errors can point to a loop, a faulty cable or a flood; record rates as a baseline.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Lists VLANs on a switch with their names, status and access ports.
commands.output: Columns VLAN, Name, Status and Ports, e.g. 10 STAFF active Gi1/0/1, Gi1/0/2.
commands.blue: Confirm ports are in the right VLAN and that unused ports are parked in a dead VLAN instead of VLAN 1.
commands.safety: Read only. Trunk ports are not listed here; use show interfaces trunk for those.

commands.what: Shows the MAC addresses the switch has learned and the port and VLAN for each.
commands.example: show mac address-table dynamic interface GigabitEthernet1/0/5
commands.output: Table of Vlan, Mac Address, Type (DYNAMIC or STATIC) and Ports.
commands.blue: Trace a suspicious IP to a physical switch port (via ARP then MAC), and spot many MACs on one access port.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Lists directly connected Cisco devices discovered with Cisco Discovery Protocol.
commands.output: Per neighbor: Device ID, IP address, Platform, Interface and Port ID, and the IOS version.
commands.blue: Map your topology and find unknown devices plugged into the network; consider disabling CDP on user facing ports.
commands.safety: Read only. CDP shares device details with anything on the link, so limit it to trusted links.

commands.what: Displays configured access control lists with per rule match counters.
commands.output: Each ACL by name or number with numbered entries such as 10 permit tcp any host 10.0.0.5 eq 443 (152 matches).
commands.blue: Verify that ACLs match policy and use the match counters to see which rules block or allow real traffic.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Shows syslog settings and the contents of the local logging buffer.
commands.output: Log lines such as %SEC_LOGIN-4-LOGIN_FAILED: Login failed [user: admin] [Source: 203.0.113.9].
commands.blue: Review login failures, interface flaps and config changes; send logs to a central syslog server or SIEM.
commands.safety: Read only. The buffer is small and is lost on reload, so forward logs off the device.

commands.what: Displays the IPv4 routing table with how each route was learned.
commands.output: A codes legend (C connected, S static, O OSPF and so on), the Gateway of last resort, then one line per route.
commands.blue: Detect unexpected routes or a changed default route that could redirect traffic.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.

commands.what: Shows the IOS version, uptime, hardware model, serial number and last reload reason.
commands.output: Cisco IOS Software version line, uptime, System image file, model, serial number and configuration register.
commands.blue: Check the version against Cisco security advisories for patching, and an unexpected reload reason can flag tampering or a crash.
commands.safety: Read only. Safe to run on systems you administer.
